docs.title: Kartoza CloudBench
docs.text:
A comprehensive cloud-native geospatial data management platform with TUI (Terminal User Interface) and Web UI for managing GeoServer, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, S3 storage, and more.

New to CloudBench? Start with Overview & Workflow for how the pieces fit together, then On-demand Conversions for turning S3 uploads into cloud-native layers.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
• Modern React interface - Beautiful Chakra UI-based web application
  • Tree browser - Hierarchical view of all GeoServer resources
  • Layer metadata editing - Comprehensive metadata management
  • GeoWebCache management - Seed, reseed, and truncate cached tiles
  • Map preview - Interactive map preview with WMS/WMTS support
  • Chunked file upload - Upload large geospatial files with progress tracking
  • S3 Storage integration - Browse and manage cloud-native geospatial data

docs.title: TUI (Terminal User Interface)
docs.text:
• Textual-based interface - Modern Python TUI with rich widgets
  • Connection manager - Store and manage multiple GeoServer connections
  • Vim-style navigation - Familiar keyboard shortcuts

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• GeoServer - Full REST API management
  • PostgreSQL/PostGIS - Direct database connections
  • S3/MinIO - Cloud storage for geospatial data
  • QGIS Server - Project management and preview
  • Terria/Cesium - 3D globe visualization

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/kartoza/kartoza-cloudbench.git
cd kartoza-cloudbench

# Using Nix (recommended)
nix develop
python manage.py runserver 8080

# Or using pip
pip install -e .
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py runserver 8080

Then visit http://localhost:8080

docs.text:

  • Backend: Python/Django with Django REST Framework

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: This guide covers deploying CloudBench in production environments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12+
  • PostgreSQL 14+ (recommended for production)
  • Reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, etc.)

docs.title: 1. Clone and Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/kartoza/kartoza-cloudbench.git
cd kartoza-cloudbench
pip install -e .

docs.title: 2. Configure Environment
docs.text:
Create /etc/cloudbench/env:

DEBUG=false
SECRET_KEY=your-secure-random-key-here
ALLOWED_HOSTS=cloudbench.example.com
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/cloudbench

docs.title: 3. Database Setup
docs.text:
# Create database
createdb cloudbench

# Run migrations
python manage.py migrate

# Create admin user
python manage.py createsuperuser

docs.title: 4. Collect Static Files
docs.text: python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

docs.title: 5. Run with Gunicorn
docs.text:
gunicorn cloudbench.wsgi:application \
    --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 \
    --workers 4 \
    --threads 2

docs.title: 6. Nginx Configuration
docs.text:
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name cloudbench.example.com;

    location /static/ {
        alias /path/to/cloudbench/staticfiles/;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

docs.title: Systemd Service
docs.text:
Create /etc/systemd/system/cloudbench.service:

[Unit]
Description=CloudBench Web Application
After=network.target postgresql.service

[Service]
User=cloudbench
Group=cloudbench
WorkingDirectory=/opt/cloudbench
EnvironmentFile=/etc/cloudbench/env
ExecStart=/opt/cloudbench/venv/bin/gunicorn cloudbench.wsgi:application --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 --workers 4
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Enable and start:

systemctl enable cloudbench
systemctl start cloudbench

docs.text:

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text: CloudBench can be deployed using Docker and Docker Compose.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: docker compose up -d

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
version: '3.8'

services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - DEBUG=false
      - SECRET_KEY=${SECRET_KEY}
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@db:5432/cloudbench
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgis/postgis:16-3.4
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DB=cloudbench
      - POSTGRES_USER=postgres
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:

docs.title: Building the Image
docs.text: docker build -t ghcr.io/kartoza/kartoza-cloudbench:latest .

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Pass environment variables via:

docker run -e SECRET_KEY=xxx -e DEBUG=false ghcr.io/kartoza/kartoza-cloudbench

Or use an env file:

docker run --env-file .env ghcr.io/kartoza/kartoza-cloudbench

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: CloudBench exposes a REST API under /api/.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Currently, the API supports session authentication. API tokens are planned.

docs.title: List Connections
docs.text:
GET /api/connections

Response: 

[
  {
    "id": "conn_123",
    "name": "Local GeoServer",
    "url": "http://localhost:8600/geoserver",
    "is_active": true
  }
]

docs.title: Create Connection
docs.text:
POST /api/connections
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "My GeoServer",
  "url": "http://geoserver.example.com/geoserver",
  "username": "admin",
  "password": "geoserver"
}

docs.title: List Workspaces
docs.text: GET /api/workspaces/{conn_id}

docs.title: Create Workspace
docs.text:
POST /api/workspaces/{conn_id}
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "my_workspace"
}

docs.title: List Layers
docs.text: GET /api/layers/{conn_id}/{workspace}

docs.title: Get Layer Details
docs.text: GET /api/layers/{conn_id}/{workspace}/{layer}

docs.title: Get Layer Styles
docs.text:
GET /api/layerstyles/{conn_id}/{workspace}/{layer}

Response: 

{
  "defaultStyle": "polygon",
  "additionalStyles": ["line", "point"]
}

docs.title: Start Preview Session
docs.text:
POST /api/preview/
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "connId": "conn_123",
  "workspace": "topp",
  "layerName": "states"
}

Response: 

{
  "url": "/api/preview/abc-123"
}

docs.title: Get Layer Info
docs.text: GET /api/preview/{session_id}/api/layer

docs.title: Get Layer Metadata
docs.text: GET /api/preview/{session_id}/api/metadata

docs.title: Initialize Upload
docs.text:
POST /api/upload/init
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "connectionId": "conn_123",
  "workspace": "topp",
  "filename": "data.gpkg",
  "fileSize": 1048576,
  "chunkSize": 5242880
}

docs.title: Upload Chunk
docs.text:
POST /api/upload/chunk
Content-Type: multipart/form-data

sessionId: abc-123
chunkIndex: 0
chunk: <binary data>

docs.title: Complete Upload
docs.text:
POST /api/upload/complete
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "sessionId": "abc-123"
}

docs.title: Error Responses
docs.text:
All errors return JSON:

{
  "error": "Description of the error"
}

HTTP status codes: - 400: Bad request - 401: Unauthorized - 404: Not found - 500: Server error

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: CloudBench has two test layers: fast unit tests that run anywhere, and staging browser tests that drive a real CloudBench through its web UI.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Run the suite with pytest:

pytest                 # or: make test  (inside the Docker stack)

CI also checks formatting and lint — match it before pushing, formatting only the files you changed:

black <files-you-changed>
ruff check .

Notes:

  • Use time.monotonic() for durations and deadlines, timezone.now() for stored timestamps. Don't patch time.monotonic in tests — set the relevant timeout setting instead.
  • Migrations are made by the maintainer; don't run makemigrations.

docs.title: Staging browser tests
docs.text: tests/staging/ drives staging CloudBench through its real UI with Playwright — logging in, clicking through the tree, uploading files, and following the S3 on-demand conversions end to end. Everything is discovered from staging itself (the connections already added, the server sizes in stock); .env.staging holds only switches.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Copy the template and fill it in:
cp .env.staging.example .env.staging
  1. Capture a login. Either let Playwright log in once:
.venv/bin/python tests/staging/browser_login.py

or, if that's slow, copy the token from your own browser's DevTools (localStorage key token on the CloudBench origin) into .staging-token and build the auth file:

.venv/bin/python tests/staging/token_from_file.py

Both write .staging-auth.json (git-ignored). The login lasts the working day; re-run when it expires.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
.venv/bin/pytest tests/staging

Everything is skipped cleanly when you are not logged in.

docs.title: What the tests cover
docs.text:
Test Area test_01_smoke App loads, connections and tools are discoverable test_02_geoserver GeoServer upload test_03_postgis PostGIS import test_04_geonode GeoNode upload (and the title applied after import) test_05_s3_on_demand GeoTIFF → COG on demand test_06_s3_invalid_on_demand A corrupt file fails cleanly; the server is still deleted test_07_s3_pmtiles_on_demand Vector → PMTiles + GeoParquet test_08_s3_copc_on_demand LAS → COPC test_09_s3_mosaic_on_demand Several tiles → one COG mosaic test_10_s3_geopackage_on_demand Skips: GeoPackage inspect is deferred on demand

The sample files they upload come from tests/staging/manual-test-data/ — regenerate them with GDAL:

python tests/staging/manual-test-data/generate.py   # add --large for the size tests

docs.title: Two rules
docs.text:
• Each on-demand test starts a real Hetzner server (billed per started hour) and deletes it when the job ends. Keep STAGING_ONDEMAND_MAX_JOBS sane and don't leave runs looping.
  • The tests never delete anything in S3, not even their own uploads. Runs are named with a timestamped prefix (cbtest_<date>_<time>_…) so they don't collide; clean-up, if any, is done by hand.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • On-demand Conversions — the feature under test, from the user's side.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Services
docs.text:
PostgreSQL connections are configured via the standard ~/.pg_service.conf file:

[production]
host=db.example.com
port=5432
dbname=geodata
user=geouser
password=secret

[development]
host=localhost
port=5432
dbname=geodata_dev
user=postgres
password=postgres

These services appear in the CloudBench sidebar under "PostgreSQL Services".

docs.title: GeoServer Connections
docs.text:
GeoServer connections are stored in the database and can be managed through:

  1. Web UI: Click the + button next to "GeoServer Connections"
  2. Admin Panel: Visit /admin/ to manage connections
  3. API: POST to /api/connections

docs.text:

  3. Name: Connection name

  6. Secret Key: AWS secret key
  7. Region: AWS region (optional)

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide will help you get CloudBench running and connected to your first GeoServer instance.

docs.title: 1. Start the Server
docs.text:
# Using Nix
nix develop
python manage.py runserver 8080

# Or using pip
python manage.py runserver 8080

docs.title: 2. Open the Web UI
docs.text: Navigate to http://localhost:8080 in your browser.

docs.title: 3. Add a GeoServer Connection
docs.text:
1. In the left sidebar, find "GeoServer Connections"
  2. Click the + button to add a new connection
  3. Enter your GeoServer details:
  4. Name: A friendly name for this connection
  5. URL: Your GeoServer URL (e.g., http://localhost:8600/geoserver)
  6. Username: GeoServer admin username
  7. Password: GeoServer admin password
  8. Click Test Connection to verify
  9. Click Save to add the connection

docs.title: 4. Browse Your Data
docs.text:
Once connected, you can:

  • Expand workspaces to see data stores, coverage stores, and layers
  • Click on a layer to see its details in the right panel
  • Preview layers on an interactive map
  • Upload data to create new stores and layers

docs.title: 5. Upload Geospatial Data
docs.text:
1. Select a workspace in the tree
  2. Click the Upload button (arrow icon)
  3. Select your file (Shapefile ZIP, GeoPackage, GeoTIFF, etc.)
  4. The file will be uploaded and published automatically

docs.title: 6. Preview Layers
docs.text:
1. Click on any layer in the tree
  2. Click the Preview button (eye icon)
  3. An interactive map will appear showing your layer

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
Everything in CloudBench hangs off a connection — a saved pointer to one service. This page covers adding, testing, and editing them. For what each type is for, see Overview & Workflow.

Each connection is scoped to exactly one target — one GeoServer, one database service, one GeoNode site, one S3 bucket — so you can add several of the same type and switch between them in the tree.

docs.title: Adding a connection
docs.text:
1. In the left tree, find the connection type (GeoServer, PostgreSQL, GeoNode, or S3 Storage) and click the + beside it.
  2. Fill in the form for that type (below).
  3. Click Test — CloudBench checks it can reach the service and authenticate — then Save. A connection that fails the test is not saved.

Inside GeoHosting, the connections for your instances are usually added for you; you can still add your own.

docs.title: What each type needs
docs.text: Type Required Notes GeoServer Base URL, username, password The REST URL, e.g. https://…/geoserver. PostgreSQL/PostGIS Host, port, database, user, password The database must have PostGIS enabled to hold spatial tables. GeoNode Site URL, username, password Uploads use the GeoNode account's permissions. S3 storage Endpoint, region, bucket, access key, secret key One bucket per connection. Works with AWS S3, MinIO, and DigitalOcean Spaces.

docs.title: Testing and editing
docs.text:
• Test re-runs the reachability and auth check at any time — use it when a service was down or a password changed.
  • Edit (the pencil) changes a connection's details; CloudBench re-tests before saving.
  • Delete (the trash icon) removes the connection from CloudBench. It does not touch the service or its data — only the saved pointer.

docs.title: When a connection fails
docs.text:
• Cannot reach the service — check the URL/host and port, and that the service is up and reachable from CloudBench's network (not only from your laptop).
  • Authentication failed — re-enter the credentials; for GeoServer and GeoNode, confirm the account has the rights you need.
  • S3 errors — check the endpoint and region match the provider, and that the keys can list the bucket. A wrong region is a common cause of signature errors.

More symptoms and fixes are in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Cloud-Native Formats
docs.text:
CloudBench can convert your uploads into cloud-native formats — files laid out so a web map reads them straight from the bucket, a piece at a time, with no server in front. This page explains each one and when to use it. To produce them, see On-demand Conversions.

Format File Holds Use it for COG .tif Raster (imagery, DEM) Any raster you want to pan and zoom on the web PMTiles .pmtiles Vector tiles Rendering many features quickly at every zoom GeoParquet .parquet Vector features + attributes Querying and analysing the attribute table COPC .copc.laz LiDAR point cloud Streaming 3D points by area

docs.title: COG — Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF
docs.text: A GeoTIFF arranged into internal tiles and overviews so a viewer fetches only the tiles in view at the right resolution. It is still a normal GeoTIFF that any GIS can open. CloudBench produces a Web Mercator COG for the map preview.

docs.title: PMTiles
docs.text: A single file of pre-rendered vector tiles. One HTTP file, read by range requests, serves a whole tiled layer — no tile server. Best when a layer has too many features to draw one by one.

docs.title: GeoParquet
docs.text: A columnar table of features with their geometry and attributes. It is the form to reach for when the question is about the data — filtering, counting, joining — rather than drawing it. CloudBench writes a GeoParquet alongside the PMTiles for a vector upload, so you get both the map and the table.

docs.title: COPC — Cloud Optimized Point Cloud
docs.text: A LAZ point cloud organised as an octree so a viewer streams just the points in view. Produced from .las/.laz uploads.

docs.title: How they relate to the preview
docs.text: Each converted layer previews on the map or in a table without a backing server (see Layer Preview): COGs and PMTiles draw on the map, GeoParquet opens as a table (and on the map), and COPC draws as a 3D point cloud. The outputs are standard files, so you can also hand the bucket folder to QGIS, GDAL, or any tool that reads these formats.

docs.title: GeoNode Uploads
docs.text: A GeoNode connection lets you upload a dataset to a GeoNode site and set its title and abstract in the same step. For adding the connection, see Connections.

docs.title: Uploading a dataset
docs.text:
1. Select a GeoNode connection and click Upload.
  2. Choose the file (a vector or raster GeoNode accepts; a shapefile goes as its components or a single-shapefile ZIP).
  3. Set the title and, optionally, an abstract.
  4. Upload. CloudBench sends the file to GeoNode and reports when the import finishes.

docs.title: Titles and abstracts
docs.text:
GeoNode imports a dataset under a name derived from the file, and does not apply a title or abstract sent with the upload itself. So CloudBench sets them in a second step: once the import finishes, it updates the new dataset with the title and abstract you entered.

Because that happens just after the import completes, the title may appear a moment later than the dataset:

  • If the dataset shows the filename briefly, give it a few seconds and refresh.
  • If the title never updates, the account may lack permission to edit the dataset, or the import may not have finished — check the dataset in GeoNode.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Uploads and the title update use the connected GeoNode account's permissions. If a dataset uploads but can't be edited, that account can't modify it in GeoNode either.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Upload rejected for size. GeoNode enforces its own upload size limit, separate from CloudBench's.
  • Dataset appears but is empty or broken. Check the file's coordinate system and that the format is one GeoNode supports.

More general symptoms are in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: On-demand Conversions
docs.text:
When you upload a file to an S3 connection, CloudBench can convert it to a cloud-native format — one that a web map can read directly from the bucket, a piece at a time, without a server in front of it. The conversion runs on CloudNativeGIS, and in on-demand mode each job gets its own server, started just for that job and deleted as soon as it finishes.

This page explains what gets converted, how to run a conversion, what it costs, and the current limits. For where the outputs land and how to view them, see Layer Preview.

docs.title: What gets converted
docs.text:
You upload You get Good for GeoTIFF (.tif) Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) Rasters, DEMs, imagery Several GeoTIFF tiles One COG mosaic (+ a VRT and a STAC catalog) A scene split into tiles Vector (.shp/.zip, .geojson, .gpkg, .kml, …) GeoParquet and PMTiles (+ a thumbnail) Features: a table and map tiles Point cloud (.las/.laz) COPC (.copc.laz) LiDAR / 3D points

Each conversion publishes into its own folder in the bucket, registers the layer in the bucket's catalog, and leaves a thumbnail so it previews on the map.

docs.title: Two modes
docs.text:
CloudBench runs conversions one of two ways, chosen by whoever configured it:

  • Fixed (non-demand) — every job runs on one standing CloudNativeGIS server. Nothing is billed per job; there is no server to pick.
  • On-demand — each job runs on a fresh server that GeoHosting starts for it and deletes when it is done. You pick the server size and confirm the cost. This is the mode used inside GeoHosting.

The rest of this page describes on-demand. The difference you see is the server picker and the cost confirmation in the upload dialog.

docs.title: Running a conversion
docs.text:
1. Select an S3 connection in the tree and click Upload.
  2. Choose your file. CloudBench detects the type and shows Convert to Cloud-Native with the matching target format.
  3. Pick a server type. The list shows each enabled size with its specs and price per hour; out-of-stock sizes can't be picked.
  4. (Optional) Set the destination key/prefix, a licence, or — for several GeoTIFFs — a mosaic name.
  5. Click Upload. A cost confirmation appears ("the server is billed per started hour and destroyed after the job"); click Continue.
  6. Watch the job. The dialog reports each stage and refreshes the bucket listing when it finishes. You can close the dialog — the job keeps running.

The Server type picker and the cost confirmation are what set on-demand apart from fixed mode; the price shown (for example 0.0176 EUR/h) is Hetzner's plus a margin.

docs.title: What happens behind the scenes
docs.text:
A conversion moves through these stages, and you can follow them on the job:

provisioning → pushing → polling → verifying → publishing → deprovisioning → completed
  • provisioning — GeoHosting starts a Hetzner server for the job and waits for it to be healthy.
  • pushing / polling — CloudBench hands CloudNativeGIS a link to your file and polls until the conversion is done.
  • verifying / publishing — the outputs are checked and written to the bucket, and the layer is added to the catalog.
  • deprovisioning — the server is deleted. This happens whether the job succeeded or failed, so a failed job never leaves a server running.

If a job fails, it fails cleanly: it records an error, publishes nothing half-made, and still deletes its server.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Each on-demand job runs one server, billed by Hetzner per started hour — so even a one-minute conversion costs a whole hour of the size you picked. The price you see in the picker is Hetzner's price plus a margin set on GeoHosting. The server is deleted as soon as the job ends, so you pay for one job's worth, not an idle machine.

Tips to keep cost down:

  • Pick the smallest size that fits the job.
  • Batch tiles into one mosaic upload instead of many single COGs.
  • Remember that a cancelled or failed job still used a started hour.

docs.title: Cancelling
docs.text: You can cancel a job while it is still pending, pushing, or polling (not once it is verifying or publishing). It stops at its next step, deletes its server, and is marked cancelled. A GeoPackage's paired jobs are cancelled together.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text:
• GeoPackage conversion is not available in on-demand mode. A GeoPackage is meant to convert as two jobs (its vector layers → PMTiles, its raster tables → COG) chosen in a picker after the file is inspected. Inspection has no server to run on in on-demand mode, so the upload reports an error ("Pick a server to run the conversion on", or a 502 from the inspect step). Use the fixed mode for GeoPackages, or convert their layers separately.
  • One server per job. A GeoPackage's two jobs (in fixed mode) use one server each, run one after the other, not a shared server.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: On-demand mode and its limits are set by an administrator. The relevant settings — CLOUDNATIVEGIS_ON_DEMAND, the GeoHosting OAuth client, and the conversion timeouts — are documented under Environment Variables. The pipeline itself is described in Architecture.

docs.title: Overview & Workflow
docs.text:
CloudBench is a workbench for geospatial data. From one web interface you connect to the services that hold your data — GeoServer, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, GeoNode, and S3 object storage — then browse, upload, convert, and preview layers without leaving the page.

This page is the map of how CloudBench fits together and the path a typical task follows. For installing or deploying it, see Getting Started; for each screen in detail, see the rest of the User Guide.

docs.title: Where CloudBench runs
docs.text:
CloudBench runs in two places, and both use the same interface:

  • Standalone — you open the web UI directly (see Quick Start) and sign in.
  • Inside GeoHosting — you open GeoHosting and click CloudBench. It loads in a panel and signs you in automatically with a token that lasts the working day. This is where on-demand conversions (below) are available, because GeoHosting supplies the servers they run on.

docs.title: The four connection types
docs.text:
Everything in CloudBench hangs off a connection — a saved pointer to one service, shown in the tree on the left. Each type does a different job:

Connection What it manages Typical use GeoServer Workspaces, stores, layers, styles, tile caches Publish and style layers, seed tiles PostgreSQL/PostGIS Database services and their tables Import vector data into a spatial database GeoNode A GeoNode site's datasets Upload datasets with titles and metadata S3 storage One bucket of cloud-native files Store and convert COG, PMTiles, GeoParquet, COPC

A connection is scoped to exactly one target — one GeoServer, one database, one bucket — so you can add several of the same type and switch between them.

docs.title: The general workflow
docs.text:
Most work in CloudBench follows the same five steps:

  1. Add a connection. Click the + next to a connection type and fill in the service's URL and credentials. CloudBench tests it before saving. In GeoHosting, the connections for your instances are usually added already.
  2. Browse. Expand the connection in the tree to see what it holds — workspaces and layers, database tables, bucket folders and objects.
  3. Upload or import. Use the Upload button to send a file to the target. For S3, you can also convert the file to a cloud-native format in the same step (see On-demand Conversions).
  4. Preview. Click a layer or object to open it on a map, in a 3D view, or as a table (see Layer Preview).
  5. Use and share. Style it in GeoServer, serve it as tiles, or hand the bucket folder to another tool — the converted outputs are standard files.
  Add a          Browse the         Upload / convert        Preview        Use / share
  connection  →  tree          →    (GeoServer, PostGIS  →  on a map  →    (styles, tiles,
                                     GeoNode, or S3)         or table       catalog, download)

docs.title: What makes CloudBench's S3 different
docs.text: For the other three connection types, CloudBench is a management front end for an existing service. S3 is more: besides browsing and uploading, it can convert your data into cloud-native formats that stream straight from the bucket — Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG), PMTiles, GeoParquet, and COPC point clouds — and preview them on the map. That conversion is what On-demand Conversions covers.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common symptoms and what to check. Page-specific troubleshooting also lives in File Uploads and Layer Preview.

docs.title: Sign-in and sessions
docs.text:
• Signed out during the day (inside GeoHosting). The token that signs you in automatically lasts the working day. When it expires, the page returns to the login screen; reopen CloudBench from GeoHosting to get a fresh one.
  • "Unknown error" loading the dashboard. Usually the sign-in token is missing or stale — reload the page, or reopen CloudBench from GeoHosting.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
• A connection won't save. It failed its test. See Connections → When a connection fails.
  • S3 signature errors. The endpoint or region is usually wrong for the provider; confirm both match the bucket.

docs.title: Uploads and conversions
docs.text:
• Upload fails or stalls. Check the file size limit (GeoNode has its own), that the format is supported, and the target service's logs. "No data came for 60 seconds" means the connection dropped — upload again.
  • Shapefile rejected. Select the .shp, .shx, and .dbf together (add .prj for the projection), or upload a ZIP with exactly one shapefile. A lone .shp is not enough.
  • "Pick a server to run the conversion on." An on-demand conversion needs a server size selected in the upload dialog. Pick one, then upload.
  • No server sizes to pick, or all out of stock. The enabled sizes are out of stock at the provider; try again later or ask an administrator to enable another size.
  • GeoPackage conversion errors in on-demand mode. This is a known limit — GeoPackage inspection isn't available on demand. See On-demand Conversions → Current limits.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
• Blank map, no layer. Reopen the preview. If a raster never appears, its extent may be unreadable; try downloading and checking the file in a GIS.
  • "Failed to fetch" / "Request failed" on a preview or README. The viewer couldn't read the file from the bucket. Recent CloudBench reads these through its own proxy to avoid this; if you still see it, make sure you are on the current build.
  • Point cloud (COPC) preview is blank. Like the other formats, a .copc.laz is streamed through CloudBench's own proxy, so a blank preview usually means you are on an older build — make sure you are on the current one. If it stays blank on the current build, the file's extent may be unreadable; downloading it and opening it in a desktop GIS confirms the data is intact.
  • Layer in the wrong place. Check its coordinate system and bounding box.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Collect the exact message, what you clicked, and the file or connection involved, and check the service's own logs (GeoServer, GeoNode, the database). For reporting issues, see Contributing.

docs.title: S3 Cloud-Native Options
docs.text:
For the full picture of cloud-native conversion — every source/output pair, the per-job on-demand servers, cost, job stages, and limits — see On-demand Conversions. This section covers the fixed (non-demand) CloudNativeGIS flow.

For S3 uploads, selecting a .shp file or a zipped shapefile (.zip) shows PMTiles under Convert to Cloud-Native when CloudNativeGIS is reachable. Cloudbench checks the service from Django using CLOUDNATIVEGIS_URL; an unreachable service hides the option without blocking normal uploads.

PMTiles is the default recommendation when available, replacing GeoParquet for shapefile uploads. Select or drag the matching .shp, .shx, and .dbf files together; include .prj for the projection. Cloudbench creates the ZIP automatically before sending it to CloudNativeGIS. A lone .shp is not enough: the browser cannot automatically read companion files you have not selected. You can also supply an existing ZIP with exactly one shapefile. Nested shapefile folders in ZIPs are flattened before forwarding. With conversion switched off, selected shapefile components are uploaded to S3 as a ZIP instead.

Cloudbench uploads the layer to CloudNativeGIS, waits for the import to succeed and the PMTiles file to be ready, then downloads it and uploads it to the selected S3 bucket. The original ZIP is not uploaded to S3. The object key keeps its prefix and replaces .zip or .shp.zip with .pmtiles. The dialog reports each stage, refreshes the S3 listing on completion, and displays conversion errors.

If the CloudNativeGIS instance requires one, its bearer token is configured server-side via CLOUDNATIVEGIS_API_TOKEN. The default conversion wait timeout is 30 minutes, configurable with CLOUDNATIVEGIS_CONVERSION_TIMEOUT; polling defaults to 5 seconds via CLOUDNATIVEGIS_POLL_INTERVAL.

Conversion continues if the dialog is closed. Cloudbench tracks jobs in its Django database, but the background thread does not survive a Django restart; interrupted jobs eventually report failure and must be retried. Local temporary files are removed after processing. The created layer remains in CloudNativeGIS for inspection.

docs.title: GeoPackage
docs.text:
A GeoPackage can hold several vector layers and raster tables in one file. When you upload one for cloud-native conversion, CloudBench inspects it and shows a picker so you choose which layers and tables to convert; the vector layers become PMTiles + GeoParquet and the raster tables become COGs, as one layer group.

Inspection is not available in on-demand mode — see the limits in On-demand Conversions. Use the fixed mode for GeoPackages, or convert their layers as separate files.
